strengths: The paper provides a reasonably careful theoretical derivation connecting a dynamic 'kinetic-energy-like' objective for discrete flow matching to an equivalent Kantorovich/minibatch-OT formulation (Theorem 3.1), generalizing the Benamou-Brenier correspondence to categorical convex-interpolant flows, with detailed proofs in the appendix.

The identification that the discrete-metric case reduces to Hamming distance and the embedding-based similarity case reduces to an L2 cost is a clean and intuitive result that connects nicely to standard continuous flow matching intuitions.

The derivation of an upper bound on perplexity for discrete flow models (Theorem 4.1, following an Opper & Sanguinetti-style variational argument) addresses a genuine gap, since discrete flows lack an analogue of the continuous change-of-variables formula for exact likelihood/perplexity estimation.

The work situates itself clearly with respect to related literature (Gat et al. 2024, Campbell et al. 2024, Tong et al. 2023, Lou et al. 2024) and reuses established notation, aiding readability for someone familiar with discrete flow matching.
weaknesses: There are no experiments anywhere in the paper: no empirical evaluation of the proposed minibatch-OT training objective, no computed perplexity numbers using the derived bound, and no comparison to autoregressive or other discrete diffusion/flow baselines, despite the abstract explicitly claiming the perplexity bound 'enables performance evaluation and comparison with other methods.' This is a critical gap for a paper making practical claims about improving generation quality and enabling evaluation.

One of the three listed 'contributions' (chains of discrete flows) is presented only as an idea in a section explicitly titled 'Future Work,' with no formalization, algorithm, or results — it should not be counted as a contribution of this submission.

The practical algorithm for solving/approximating the minibatch OT coupling (e.g., Sinkhorn or Hungarian-style matching over sequences, complexity considerations, how similarity/cost matrices are computed and updated during training) is not specified; the 'Training Stability' discussion is speculative ('could for example... using a moving average') rather than a concrete, tested method.

The tightness or usefulness of the perplexity upper bound is never empirically or even numerically illustrated (e.g., on a toy distribution), so it is unclear whether the bound is practically informative or vacuously loose, which undermines the claimed evaluation utility.

The proposed source-distribution modifications (token-marginal or K-means-based source distributions) are introduced but never justified quantitatively or theoretically beyond intuition, and their interaction with the OT objective is not analyzed.

Presentation is dense and proof-heavy with limited intuition-building (e.g., diagrams, toy examples) for readers less familiar with the technical machinery, and the lack of any concrete algorithmic pseudocode makes reproducibility essentially impossible from the current text.

strengths: The paper tackles two genuinely open and relevant problems in discrete flow matching: (1) how to design a rectification/path-simplification analogue in the absence of deterministic sample paths, and (2) how to obtain a tractable likelihood proxy (perplexity) for discrete flow models, given the lack of an instantaneous change-of-variables formula.

The derivation connecting a dynamic 'kinetic-energy-like' objective for discrete flows to an equivalent Kantorovich formulation is a natural and interesting extension of the Benamou-Brenier theorem to categorical state spaces, and the special cases recovering the Hamming distance and L2 embedding distance as transport costs are intuitive and satisfying.

The perplexity upper bound (Theorem 4.1 and its instantiation in Eq. 20-24) is derived carefully by adapting the Markov-jump-process variational bound of Opper & Sanguinetti (2007), paralleling the approach used by Lou et al. (2024) for discrete diffusion, and is presented with a full proof in the appendix.

The identification of practical difficulties (e.g., poor minibatch matching quality when the source distribution is uninformative, need to decouple embeddings used for coupling vs. training) shows the authors are aware of the practical gap between the theory and deployment.
weaknesses: The manuscript contains absolutely no experiments. Neither the minibatch-OT training objective nor the perplexity bound is evaluated on any dataset, synthetic or real, so none of the central claims (that minibatch OT reduces the number of jumps and improves generation quality, or that the perplexity bound is a useful/tight tool for 'evaluation and comparison with other methods' as claimed in the abstract) are empirically supported. For a paper whose stated goal is to enable model evaluation and comparison, presenting zero comparisons is a fundamental deficiency.

Section 5 ('Future Work: Chains of Discrete Flows') is explicitly speculative and untested, yet it is listed as one of the paper's three main contributions in the introduction; this inflates the perceived contribution beyond what is actually delivered.

The practical guidance offered (choice of source distribution via token marginals or K-means, embedding decoupling/moving-average stabilization for training stability) is presented as informal discussion without any theoretical guarantee or empirical validation, weakening confidence that these suggestions are actually beneficial.

No discussion of the tightness of the perplexity bound, computational cost of evaluating it (the bound requires integrating over t and enumerating xt-dependent sums, and its practicality for large V and L is unclear), or how it compares numerically to true/other approximate likelihoods.

The paper does not engage with or empirically compare to existing discrete diffusion/flow perplexity estimators (e.g., Lou et al. 2024's ELBO for SEDD) despite building directly on that approach, so it is unclear whether the proposed bound is tighter, looser, or comparable in practice.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy with minor grammatical issues (e.g., 'less ambitions' in Section 5), and the core theoretical contributions, while lengthy, are incremental adaptations of known techniques (minibatch OT of Tong et al./Fatras et al., Benamou-Brenier, and Opper-Sanguinetti variational bound) to the discrete-flow setting rather than fundamentally new machinery.
Reproducibility is not applicable/assessable since there is no code, no experimental protocol, and no dataset used to substantiate any claim.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and interesting problem gap: the rectification strategy central to continuous flow matching does not transfer to discrete flow matching because sample paths are stochastic, and the paper proposes a principled alternative objective for reducing state transitions.

Derives a Kantorovich (static) formulation equivalent to a dynamic-OT-like objective for discrete flows with convex/linear interpolants, with detailed step-by-step proofs in the appendix, and shows two natural special cases (discrete metric -> Hamming distance cost; L2 embedding metric -> L2 cost), which is an elegant and interpretable result.

Derives a novel upper bound on perplexity for discrete flow matching models by adapting the Markov-chain KL-divergence bound of Opper & Sanguinetti (2007), addressing the genuine lack of an instantaneous-change-of-variables analogue for discrete flows and providing (in principle) a tool for likelihood-based evaluation and comparison with autoregressive/diffusion baselines.

Proposes concrete, easy-to-implement heuristics for improving minibatch coupling quality (marginal-token source distribution, K-means-based source distribution), grounded in the theoretical analysis of when minibatch OT should help.
weaknesses: The paper contains zero empirical results: there is no experiment demonstrating that the proposed minibatch-OT training objective actually reduces the number of state transitions, improves generation quality, or reduces the number of sampling steps needed, despite this being the stated primary motivation of the work.

The proposed perplexity upper bound is likewise never evaluated empirically -- its tightness, computational cost, and usefulness for comparing against existing discrete diffusion/flow perplexity estimates (e.g., Lou et al. 2024, Campbell et al. 2024, Sahoo et al. 2024) are not demonstrated on any dataset.

Section 5 ('Future Work: Chains of Discrete Flows') is included as a main body section but is purely speculative, with no derivation completed or experiment run, and explicitly states 'it remains to be tested' -- this signals the submission is incomplete for a main-track venue.

The claimed analogy to the Benamou-Brenier theorem is overstated: unlike the continuous theorem, which minimizes over arbitrary velocity fields, the discrete 'dynamic formulation' is derived only for a fixed conditional interpolant family (Eq. 9), so the result is closer to an identity for a restricted class of flows than a full categorical analogue of the classical theorem; this distinction is not clearly acknowledged.

The 'Training Stability' discussion (decoupling embeddings used for minibatch coupling vs. the network) is hand-wavy and not accompanied by a concrete algorithm, ablation, or convergence analysis, despite the paper itself noting a nontrivial coupled-optimization instability concern.

There is no discussion of reproducibility artifacts (code, pseudocode, hyperparameters, datasets) since no experiments are run; a reader cannot verify or build upon the practical impact of the theoretical contributions.

Limited engagement with how the minibatch strategy performs relative to prior minibatch-OT results in continuous flow matching (Tong et al., 2023) when applied to the discrete embedding space, and no discussion of computational overhead of computing minibatch couplings for sequence data with large vocabularies/lengths.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: the paper derives a categorical Benamou-Brenier-type theorem for discrete flow matching with convex interpolants, generalizing beyond the classical quadratic-cost setting to arbitrary similarity measures s(x^i, x_t^i), with full proofs provided in the appendix (Theorem 3.1, Corollaries 3.2/3.3).

Two new upper bounds on perplexity for DFM are derived by extending techniques from discrete diffusion (Opper & Sanguinetti, Haxholli et al.) to the DFM setting; these are shown to reduce to known special cases (MD4 bound) as sanity checks, lending credibility to the derivations.

The multimask flow (DFM-MMLM) is a clever and practically useful device that enables meaningful OT couplings while preserving the beneficial time-independence property of masked flows (proven in Appendix A.6), bridging the gap between best-performing masked models and OT-compatible flows.

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple scales: small-scale proof-of-concept (Shakespeare/Morse), bound-tightness studies in toy settings, and realistic GPT-2-scale experiments on OpenWebText with multiple downstream evaluation corpora (Lambada, Wikitext, PTB, LM1B).

Careful empirical diligence: standard deviations, entropy-based diversity checks (showing OT does not cause mode collapse, unlike known issues in SEDD), dual-judge evaluation (GPT2-Large and Llama 3.1 8B), correlation analysis between the derived bound and generative perplexity (Pearson r=0.96), and scaling/overhead analysis of minibatch OT with respect to batch size and sequence length.

The paper is transparent about limitations, including honestly noting that bound estimation for OT-trained models is only an approximation and that the interacting optimization between coupling and embeddings could destabilize training, alongside proposing future mitigations.
weaknesses: The headline claim of an '8-fold' reduction in inference steps is achieved specifically in the BoW-source setting, which the paper itself acknowledges is not competitive with the best-performing masked-style flows (e.g., DFM-B family perplexities are substantially worse than DFM-MMLM family in Table 3); this somewhat overstates the practical significance relative to the more relevant multimask setting, where gains from OT are much more modest (e.g., only ~3.5% improvement at 1024 steps between DFM-N and DFM-MMLM-OT).

The tightness of the two proposed perplexity bounds is only evaluated in a toy 3-token, length-2 vocabulary setting (Appendix C.5); no assessment of bound tightness is provided for the realistic GPT-2-scale models actually used for the paper's main comparisons, leaving open how reliable the 'principled evaluation' claim is at scale.

Multimask flow doubles the effective vocabulary size (100,514 tokens), which likely incurs non-trivial extra computational/memory cost (e.g., larger softmax), but this overhead is not clearly quantified or discussed relative to standard masked DFM.

Some experimental comparisons are limited to a single dataset (OpenWebText) and a single model scale (GPT-2-sized), so it is unclear whether the reported benefits of minibatch OT and multimask flows generalize to larger models or other domains.

The core theoretical result, while technically sound, is a fairly natural extension of existing minibatch-OT flow-matching ideas (Tong et al. 2024) and the DFM framework (Gat et al. 2024); the degree of novelty is somewhat incremental, and concurrent work (Shaul et al., 2025) is noted to derive a similar bound via a different route, which is appropriately acknowledged but slightly tempers claims of originality.

The paper is extremely dense with heavy notation and lengthy derivations, which, combined with the large appendix, may hinder reproducibility and comprehension for readers without significant background in both discrete flow matching and optimal transport theory.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: discrete flow matching lacks an analogue of rectified flows and instantaneous change-of-variables likelihood estimation, and the authors propose principled fixes for both gaps.

The theoretical derivation connecting a weighted path-length dynamic objective to a Kantorovich static formulation (Theorem 3.1) is carried out in careful, complete detail, with clean corollaries recovering Hamming distance and L2 cost as special cases.

The two perplexity upper bounds (Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.4) generalize known discrete-diffusion bounds (Lou et al. 2024; Haxholli et al. 2025) to the DFM setting, and the paper shows these bounds coincide with the known MD4 objective in the masked special case, lending some external validation.

The empirical section is reasonably broad: toy Shakespeare/Morse experiments, GPT-2-scale OpenWebText experiments with multiple downstream test sets (Lambada, PTB, Wikitext, LM1B), ablations on OT solver/batch size, and scaling/overhead measurements.
The multi-mask flow idea is a sensible practical mechanism to allow non-trivial couplings (and hence OT) while retaining the time-independence property of standard masked flows.

The tightness of the perplexity bound is at least partially examined analytically and empirically in simplified settings, and correlation between the bound and generative perplexity is reported (0.96), which is a good-faith attempt at validating the bound's usefulness.
weaknesses: The authors' own Remark 3.4 concedes that the 'Benamou–Brenier-type theorem' is a pointwise identity that holds before any optimization is performed (since the flow is fully determined by the coupling), which substantially weakens the claimed novelty/depth of the theoretical contribution; it is closer to a change-of-formula identity than a genuine variational optimal-transport result.

The perplexity bounds are derived by dropping a term (Eq. 140) whose magnitude is untested in the realistic, large-vocabulary, GPT2-scale regime where the bounds are actually used for model comparison; the only tightness quantification (11% gap) comes from a toy 3-token, length-2 vocabulary, leaving the practical reliability of the bound-based comparisons with SEDD/GPT-2 (Table 2) largely unverified.

The headline '8x reduction in inference steps' result is specific to a BoW source distribution, which is a somewhat artificial setting; the practically preferred masked-source flows cannot use OT directly, and the fix (multi-mask flow) only yields modest generative perplexity gains (e.g., 147.07 to 141.92 at 1024 steps in Table 3), undercutting the headline claim's broader significance.

Doubling the vocabulary size to Vs=50,257 mask tokens for multi-mask flow is a substantial architectural change whose true cost (extra embedding parameters, memory, compute) is not clearly isolated or discussed against the modest performance gains it provides.

Several scaling claims in Section 5.4 (e.g., that OT overhead 'should drop below 1.9%' at L=1024, entries marked 'E' for extrapolated in Table 4) are extrapolated rather than directly measured, weakening confidence in the scalability claims.

Table 2 shows GPT-2 outperforming DFM-N/SEDD on 3 of 5 benchmarks, and the paper does not fully grapple with what this implies for the practical competitiveness of the proposed bounds/flows versus autoregressive baselines.

No direct empirical comparison to the concurrent, closely related work of Shaul et al. (2025), despite the paper noting their bound is essentially equivalent; this omission makes it hard to assess the marginal contribution over concurrent work.

The presentation is heavily proof- and appendix-dependent (14+ pages of dense derivations), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility checking by readers not willing to verify each algebraic step.

Evaluation relies solely on other language models (GPT2-Large, Llama) as generative-perplexity judges without human evaluation or additional intrinsic quality checks, which is a common but limited proxy for text quality.

strengths: The paper derives a rigorous Benamou-Brenier-type theorem for discrete flow matching with convex interpolants, showing that a path-length-oriented dynamic objective (generalizing to arbitrary similarity/cost functions s, not just squared Euclidean distance) equals a static Kantorovich formulation amenable to minibatch OT. This is a clean and non-trivial theoretical extension of continuous-flow OT ideas (Tong et al.) to the discrete/categorical setting, with full proofs provided in the appendix.

Two upper bounds on perplexity for general DFM models are derived from first principles (extending Opper & Sanguinetti and Haxholli et al.), one of which is shown to recover the MD4 bound of Shi et al. as a special case, giving a nice sanity check and unifying view of prior heuristic objectives.

Multimask flow (DFM-MM) is a simple but clever fix to the 'trivial coupling' problem of standard masked DFM (only Dirac source), enabling meaningful OT couplings while provably preserving the practically important time-independence of predictive probabilities (Proposition A.2).

Experiments span multiple scales (toy Morse/Shakespeare, GPT-2-scale on OpenWebText), include ablations on OT solver and minibatch size, timing/overhead analysis showing OT is computationally cheap (3-15% overhead) and scales favorably with sequence length and embedding dimension, and report both GPT2- and Llama-judged generative perplexity plus diversity (entropy) checks to rule out mode collapse.

The paper reports a strong empirical correlation (Pearson 0.96) between the derived perplexity bound and generative perplexity, lending practical credibility to the bound as an evaluation/training tool, and it explicitly investigates bound tightness (albeit only in small synthetic settings) rather than simply asserting usefulness.

The limitations section is honest, identifying the coupling-embedding interaction issue as an open problem, and the paper appropriately credits concurrent related work (Shaul et al., 2025) that derived a similar bound independently.
weaknesses: The headline '8-fold reduction in steps' result is obtained specifically for the BoW-source setting (DFM-B vs DFM-B-OT and DFM-MMLM vs DFM-MMLM-OT), which is a less practically relevant source distribution than masked flows; the paper does not report an analogous OT ablation for the strongest masked-flow variants (DFM-N/DFM-O) trained with OT, so the generality of the speedup claim to the best-performing setups is unclear.

Bound tightness is only empirically/theoretically examined in toy examples (3-token vocabulary, sequence length 2), leaving the actual looseness of the bounds at realistic GPT-2 scale unverified; this weakens the claim that the bounds enable 'principled' model comparison in the experiments of Section 5.2/5.3.

In Table 2/3, GPT-2 (autoregressive) clearly outperforms both SEDD and DFM-N on most benchmarks, and DFM-MM's improvement over standard masked DFM is numerically modest (e.g., ~2.5% perplexity reduction at 1024 steps), somewhat tempering the significance of the proposed contributions relative to strong baselines.

Multimask flow doubles the token vocabulary (50,257 extra mask tokens), which has embedding-table and possibly output-layer cost implications that are not clearly quantified or discussed relative to the reported ~5% overhead figures (which seem to concern only OT computation, not the added mask-token parameters).

The paper bundles three fairly distinct contributions (OT theorem, perplexity bounds, multimask flows), and the resulting density of notation/proofs in the main text (with heavy reliance on a very long appendix) somewhat hurts readability and makes it harder to isolate which specific claims each experiment supports.

Experimental variance is only reported over generated samples/test points, not over independent training runs/seeds, so it is unclear how sensitive the reported gains (e.g., DFM-MM vs DFM-MM-OT differences) are to training stochasticity.
